A Business agenda item (item 8.A) and suggested resolution for the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop on a proposed public-private partnership with the Troy Racquet Club (TRC).

TRC approached Administration and the Board proposing a partnership to expand access to tennis and pickleball for Troy students and the community by developing a tennis facility on the Troy High School site.

A Business agenda item (item 8.A) with a suggested resolution presented at the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop concerning a proposed Public-Private Partnership between the Troy School District and the Troy Racquet Club (TRC). Per the item, TRC approached Administration and presented to the Board a proposal to enter into a partnership that would expand access to tennis and pickleball for the students of Troy and the Troy community as a whole through the development of a tennis facility on the Troy High School site. The recommended action is to accept the resolution.

The resolution's whereas clauses set out the shared intent of the School District and TRC to positively impact Troy students and to expand tennis and pickleball offerings to Troy School District (TSD) students and the Troy community through a tennis facility on the Troy High School site. The design of the facility and site would seek to minimize the amount of additional concrete and traffic-flow issues and to minimize any adverse impacts to the environment through retention of current trees or planting of new trees.

Subject to design and construction approval, the facility would include 12 to 15 tennis courts, an expansion of the 8 courts that currently exist, and would be domed approximately October through April to allow for winter play, with outdoor lighting to permit later evening play in the summer. The facility would be membership-based, pay-to-play for community members and, outside of the school day, for students. In exchange, Troy High School students and staff would have free exclusive access to the facility during the tennis sections of the Physical Education curriculum, and Troy School District tennis programs would have free access to the facility for utilization during their season. TRC would provide free membership and access to the club for Troy students who show proof of economically disadvantaged status. The Board also commits to explore additional sites and opportunities to provide free access to tennis for its students and community through development of new tennis courts.

The operative resolution authorizes the Superintendent of the School District, Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate and execute a lease agreement with TRC consistent with the statements of the resolution, subject to the review and approval of the School District's legal counsel. The document includes procedural fields for Moved by, Supported by, and Yes / No vote tallies, which are blank in this workshop version.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A First Student staffing spreadsheet (sheet labeled DSR) tracking Troy School District bus-driver counts on a weekly basis from November 15, 2021 through January 2023, structured as a side-by-side 5-Tier Analysis and 3-Tier Analysis. It was included in the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop packet as part of the materials on high school start times and transportation staffing.

For each week the sheet records: Troy routes (55 under the 5-tier system, reduced to 53 beginning around August 1, 2022; 75 under the 3-tier scenario), Clawson routes (a constant 4), standby drivers needed (8 for the 5-tier case, 10 for the 3-tier case), total drivers needed, total drivers needed including Clawson, total drivers on hand including standbys, and the resulting drivers short or long (both with and without Clawson). It also tracks the recruiting pipeline each week: applications received, applicants interviewed, applicants hired, applicants on hold, employee resignations, employee terminations, and medical leaves.

Under the current 5-tier system, Troy needed roughly 63 drivers (67 including Clawson routes). Early in the period the district ran a significant shortage - about 7 to 13 drivers short from November 2021 through spring 2022 (for example, 51 drivers on hand against 63 needed in December 2021, a shortfall of about 12) - which gradually improved through 2022 as hiring caught up, reaching approximately break-even or a slight surplus by late 2022 (for example, 65 on hand for a +4 position on December 12, 2022, and small positive figures through the fall). Measured against the Clawson-inclusive need, the district generally remained a few drivers short.

Under the hypothetical 3-tier system, the sheet shows the district would need about 85 drivers (89 including Clawson) plus standbys, and with the same actual headcount would have been persistently and deeply short - on the order of 20 to 39 drivers short throughout the entire period (for example, shortfalls near -34 to -38 in late 2021 and still roughly -20 to -27 by late 2022). The data quantifies the staffing gap that a move from a 5-tier to a 3-tier transportation system would create, reinforcing the transportation department's position that a 3-tier operation could not be adequately staffed. The weekly application, interview, hire, resignation, and termination columns document the recruiting churn behind the net driver counts.

What it is
Slide deck presented to the Troy Board of Education summarizing survey data on high school start times, plus next steps and a timeline. The slides carry an internal date of March 2, 2021, though the file appears in the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop materials.

Background
- The Board had studied start times for about four years.
- In 2011, amid record-low state funding, the district moved from a 3-tier busing schedule (one start each for elementary, middle, and high schools) to a 5-tier schedule.
- The change reduced the bus fleet by 14 buses and cut transportation costs by roughly $800,000 per year, but required shifting high school start times earlier to 7:20 a.m.

Research cited
- The CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend high schools start no earlier than 8:00 a.m. (ideally 8:30 a.m. or later), citing adolescent melatonin patterns.
- Early starts are linked to lower academic achievement, higher tardiness/absenteeism/truancy, more juvenile delinquency, greater teen depression, and more teen driving accidents.

Survey
- Respondents: 3,297 parents, 2,208 students, and 878 staff.
- Questions gauged how much priority the district should place on enabling later high school starts, including a high-school-only subset.

Key results
- Rating it a 'critical problem that needs to be corrected as soon as possible': 16% of parents, 20% of students, and 21% of staff overall; 18%, 26%, and 32% respectively within the high-school-only group.

Purpose
To present community input as the Board considered returning to a 3-tier schedule so high schools could start at 8:00 a.m. or later.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation prepared for a Troy Board of Education workshop reviewing survey data on high school start times, with stated key takeaways of reviewing survey data, next steps, and a timeline. The slides carry an internal header date of March 2, 2021, but the document is filed within the April 4, 2023 Board of Education Workshop packet, apparently as background for continued study of the issue.

Background and history: The presentation explains that the Board had been studying start times for roughly four years. When state funding was cut to its lowest point in 2011, the district shifted from a 3-tier busing schedule (a single start time each for elementary, middle, and high schools) to a 5-tier schedule with staggered start times across buildings. This allowed more efficient bus use, reducing the fleet by 14 buses and cutting transportation costs by about $800,000 per year. However, to keep the latest-starting elementary buildings from dismissing near 5 p.m., the district moved high school start times earlier, to 7:20 a.m. The deck notes this created burdens: early wake-ups for teens and difficulty scheduling after-school teacher professional development and collaboration, since teachers of similar grades finished their days at different times. The district operated on this schedule from 2011 onward.

Research findings cited: National studies indicate adolescents' melatonin levels prevent them from falling asleep early enough to get healthy sleep when schools start before 8:00 a.m., with about 8:30 a.m. considered ideal. Chronic sleep loss at early-start high schools is associated with lower academic achievement across the school day, higher tardiness/absenteeism/truancy, higher rates of juvenile delinquency and arrest, more teen depression and stress-related disorders, and double-digit increases in teen driving accidents. Studies also found that students at schools shifting to later starts do get more sleep, countering the argument that teens would simply stay up later. Both the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend high schools start at 8:00 a.m. or later. The deck also lists reasons early starts persist, including cheaper and more efficient bus routing, allowing elementary and middle schools to start later, earlier extracurricular start times (noting that because Oakland County high school game times generally start after 4 p.m., a later Troy end time would not affect game times), students leaving before parents depart for work, and older students being home to provide after-school care for younger siblings.

Survey results: Respondents were 3,297 parents, 2,208 students, and 878 staff, with multiple grade-level responses allowed. Asked how much importance the district should place on finding a way to let high schools start later, 16% of parents, 20% of students, and 21% of staff called it 'a critical problem that needs to be corrected as soon as possible,' while roughly half of each group said it was not a significant problem. Among a high-school-only subset (1,360 parents, 1,670 students, 321 staff), the 'critical problem' share rose to 18% of parents, 26% of students, and 32% of staff. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Recommendation letter dated March 22, 2023 from John C. Foster, President of Convergent Technology Partners, addressed to Beth Soggs, Technology Director of the Troy School District, concerning the Elementary School Audio Systems RFP #9956.

Process: On March 3, 2023, Troy School District issued the Request for Proposal soliciting bids for Elementary School Audio Systems, posting it to the District and State websites. Convergent spoke with several viable vendors and directed them to download the RFP and supporting documentation to build a strong bidding pool. On March 21, 2023, sealed bids were accepted and opened by the district; four proposals were received. All proposals were evaluated for compliance with the RFP requirements, pricing, technical solution, and acceptance of the terms and conditions, and all were found compliant. TelSystems was determined to be the low qualified bidder. The letter notes the district had used this integrator previously for A/V consultation and small projects with good results, and that Convergent had also worked with the company before with favorable results, most recently at Rochester Community Schools installing similar systems in its elementary schools and the rest of the district.

Base bid pricing was tabulated as: TelSystems $252,300.00; Acorn $270,867.90; Moss Telecom $284,437.70; and Sound Planning $330,713.00.

Solution: The RFP was structured as a base bid with multiple alternates so the district could choose the right solution at the right price, since elementary buildings differ in layout and requirements; TelSystems also offered favorable voluntary alternates. All buildings would receive the same technology, namely stage and cafeteria systems with microphones permanently installed in the ceilings, a monitor speaker for performers, Bluetooth capability, handheld and lavalier wireless microphones, new speakers, and a ceiling-mounted camera for live streaming of events, all housed in existing stage cabinets. Buildings with a partition between the cafeteria/stage and gymnasium would receive two additional speakers to serve larger combined audiences and stand-alone use. Gymnasiums would leverage the powerful processing system in the stage cabinet to form a self-contained system with their own Bluetooth and wireless microphones, operable independently of the main stage system, reusing existing cabinets where available or adding small ones.

Recommendation: The evaluation team accepted all mandatory and voluntary alternates to achieve technical and operational parity across all elementary buildings and to replace all failed existing equipment. The cost of the alternates is $201,376.00. Foster recommends awarding the project to the low qualified bidder, TelSystems, in the amount of $453,676.00 ($252,300.00 base bid plus $201,376.00 in alternates), with an additional roughly 10% contingency of $45,000.00, for a total of $498,676.00. What it is
A presentation on adopting a new 6-8 mathematics curriculum for Troy School District, brought to the May 2, 2023 Board Workshop as the outcome of a 2019-2023 review.

Background
- Current resources (Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math) in use nearly 10 years
- Learning partners: Michael D. Steele, PhD (Univ. of Wisconsin-Milwaukee; NSF program officer); Ted Coe, PhD (VP, Academic Advocacy-Mathematics, NWEA; formerly Achieve, Inc.); Jonathan Bostic, PhD (Bowling Green State University)
- Reviewed 6th-8th grade M-STEP trends and a grade 3-7 cohort (2015-2019); students took the PSAT 8 in 2018/19

Key findings
- Finding 1: pre-COVID performance slightly declining or stagnant; fewer students at advanced/proficient, more not proficient
- Finding 2: students cannot fluidly move between tracks in middle school
- Finding 3: explore task-based, inquiry-based pedagogy that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding

Pilot
- Investigated 8 curricula, narrowed to two via a review matrix (Blue/Red/Gold/Green criteria)
- 50% of middle school math teachers piloted; all four middle schools; all courses represented (Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors, Math 8)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (May 2, 2023 Workshop) on the district's 6-8 mathematics curriculum adoption, framed as the result of a multi-year curriculum review conducted from 2019 to 2023.

Phase 1 (Research and Vision): The district noted it had used its current resources, Math Expressions and Big Ideas Math, for almost 10 years. It drew on learning partnerships with three mathematics-education scholars: Michael D. Steele, PhD (University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee professor and National Science Foundation program officer); Ted Coe, PhD (VP, Academic Advocacy-Mathematics at NWEA, and formerly Director of Mathematics at Achieve, Inc., 2014-2020); and Jonathan Bostic, PhD (professor of mathematics education at Bowling Green State University). The team examined TSD data, including 6th-, 7th-, and 8th-grade M-STEP results over time and a math cohort tracked on the M-STEP from grade 3 (2015) through grade 7 (2019); it notes that in 2018/19 students took the PSAT 8.

The work referenced the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice and the eight Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices (NCTM, 2014, 'Principles to Actions'), and articulated a vision drawn from NCTM (2020, 'Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics') that all students are doers of mathematics who develop deep understanding, critique the world through mathematics, and experience its wonder, joy, and beauty.

Three findings emerged: (1) Explore curricular changes - program data from the five years preceding COVID showed student performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students achieving advanced and proficient and an increase in those not proficient; (2) Explore course sequencing - students were not able to move fluidly between tracks in middle school; and (3) Explore classroom pedagogy - investigate task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding.

Phase 2 (Explore) centered on a curricular pilot guided by questions about aligning programming with the district's vision, building conceptual understanding, learning trajectories, task- and inquiry-based experiences, students' math identities, and teacher supports. Evaluation used a Middle School Math Curriculum Review Matrix organized by Blue, Red, Gold, and Green strands, scoring how curricula enable deep learning, discussion, inquiry/task-based work, coherent sequencing, differentiation, professional learning, research grounding, and future pathways.

Pilot process: the team investigated eight different curricula and narrowed the field to two using the review matrix. Fifty percent of the district's middle school math teachers participated, with representation from each course (Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors, and Math 8) and all four middle schools taking part. The pilot ran Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) in Semester 1 and Illustrative Mathematics (IM) in Semester 2, with two or more units of each taught. Fifty percent of the district's middle school math teachers participated, with representation from each course (Math 6, Math 6/7 Honors, Math 7, Math 7/8 Honors, Math 8), and all four middle schools participated. In Semester 1 teachers taught Connected Mathematics Project (CMP) and in Semester 2 Illustrative Mathematics (IM); two or more units of each curriculum were taught by all teachers in the pilot.

Recommendation: Illustrative Math (IM), described as problem-based, built on universal design for learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students who are ready for more, built-in instructional routines that support teachers and students, a predictable and purposeful activity and lesson structure, and practice problem sets with built-in cumulative review. The presentation walks through example Math 8 lessons involving negative exponents, describing Cool Down guidance coded for teachers as More Chances, Points Emphasize, and Press Pause, and Warm-up activities that use a Collect and Display routine to stabilize the varied mathematical language in use; it also shows a sample SAT problem and a sample AP exam question.

Middle school pathways: The document explains the choice between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1. Math 8 is described as a natural transition from a Math 7 experience, in which students explore ideas of linearity, functions, and geometry and establish a solid foundation for future Algebra 1 and Geometry, while Honors Algebra 1 embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1, with students formalizing and generalizing their understandings and a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings will host information nights to discuss and illustrate the differences between Math 8 and Honors Algebra 1, and families will engage with math teachers to discuss individual student needs, considering problem-solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking and ideas, math assessment feedback, and standardized test scores. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A report titled Middle School Mathematics Materials Adoption, dated May 2023 and submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Kate Rainey to the Troy School District Board of Education for its May 16, 2023 regular meeting. It documents the district's comprehensive review of middle school mathematics curriculum and the pilot supporting a new materials adoption.

Rationale. Troy reviews its curricular materials on roughly a nine-year cycle; the last middle school math adoption occurred in 2012. Since then the district reports a better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, the availability of better-aligned resources, and continued guidance from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM). Teachers had been supplementing the existing resource with problem-based tasks and number-sense routines, and the district sought a single resource that fully addresses both deep conceptual learning and mathematical fluency.

Process and selection. The district assembled a Middle School Math Pilot Team, an interdepartmental group with representation from every grade level and building. Members engaged with Catalyzing Change (NCTM) and Building Thinking Classrooms (Liljedahl, 2021) and continued a partnership with Professor Jonathan Bostic of Bowling Green State University. The team established a vision for mathematics teaching and learning aligned to the district strategic plan and built a rubric (organized by pillars) to vet resources. The named team members were, at Boulan: Jordan Baines (Math 6, Math 6/7), Michelle Tasich (Math 6, Math 6/7), Kristy D'Ambrosi (Math 8), and A.J. Scovoronski (Math Specialist); at Baker: Sree Bollavaram (Math 8), Jamie VanTiem (Math 7), and Andrew LaTorre (Math Specialist); at Smith: Taryn Huang (Math 6), Cherie Maher (Math 7, Math 7/8), Brad Pyke (Math 8), and Melissa Rehbine (Math Specialist); and at Larson: Wendy Wilcox (Math 6, Math 6/7), Shelley McHugh (Math 7), Hadeel Yousif (Math 8), Lyndsey Becker (Math 8), and Mark Hayes (Math Specialist).

The team previewed eight resources -- Mid-School Math; College-Preparatory Mathematics (CPM); Agile Mind; Big Ideas; Desmos; Amplify; Connected Mathematics Project (CMP); and Illustrative Mathematics (IM) -- and used the review matrix to narrow the field to two finalists: CMP and IM.

Pilot process. Each pilot teacher committed to teaching at least two units from both finalists (some taught more), with CMP used in semester one and IM in semester two. Professional learning included 1.5 days of in-school PD before each pilot, four job-embedded PL opportunities per pilot teacher, district PD featuring two days with Dr. Bostic and Michigan State University facilitators, PLC meetings supported by building substitutes, and co-planning, co-teaching, and coaching by math specialists; pilot teachers were also paid for after-hours work. Data collected included student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos, and assessments; after each pilot, teachers completed a survey on program strengths and weaknesses and revisited the review matrix.

Early reflections on CMP cited strengths such as offering students multiple ways to solve problems and deepening learning through talk and collaboration, with some teachers finding the provided support sufficient to implement with fidelity. Challenges included concerns about whether the curriculum was sufficiently invitational and relevant to students, that materials were not manageable to use and did not provide enough guidance, and about supporting the needs of all students. The extracted text is truncated before the Illustrative Mathematics reflections and the team's final recommendation.

The June 2023 Accountability Report documents progress on Troy School District's strategic plan, branded Project 2026 Blueprint, structured around a foundation of Mission (why the district exists), Vision (what it must become), Values (how staff behave), and Goals (targets and timelines). Its redesign process follows three phases: See (system-level demographic, process, academic, and perception data), Engage (planning with key stakeholders including students, the Board of Education, and staff), and Act (redesign with Strategic Planning Teams, review with the BOE, and June finalization). Progress is reported against the World Class for All pillars, each carrying objectives and key results.

Green Pillar (Early Childhood to Career): Objectives include continued investment in high-quality early childhood education, advocacy for universal preschool for three- and four-year-olds, and expanded college and career pathways offering high-quality career and technical education, expanded computer science access, connections for underrepresented students to in-demand careers, and work-based learning tied to a credential or college credit. The 2023-24 early childhood enrollment plan includes tuition-based full-day and half-day AM programs (adding sections); GSRP capped at 80 (requesting additional slots, with income-threshold expansion and a shift to Morse, Troy Union, Hill, and Wass to increase access); the free Strong Beginnings three-year-old program; PreK at 90/100 with an added section; and ECP capped at 96. Additional initiatives include a Kindergarten Transition Committee; Portrait of a Graduate (Phases 1-3 complete after a January BoE workshop, with board adoption pending); K-8 career-readiness engagement partnered with media specialists and Maker Space growth; Early Middle College with Lawrence Technological University (LTU); a Business Round Table; digital portfolios tied to Xello; and expansion of TSD Learning Portfolios to Grades 3-9. Cited challenges include preschool access barriers and building buy-in; June 2023 recommendations include ongoing preschool recruitment, a Preschool Summer Institute 2023, prioritizing digital citizenship K-8, and jump-starting a K-12 computer science curriculum collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team.

Red Pillar (Equity and Well-Being): Objectives center on funding additional investments to support the whole child and elevating a focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency district-wide. Reported celebrations and key results from January-June 2023 include re-establishing and re-energizing the pillar; establishing a district-level equity team (JEDI Council) and an equity webpage; a Tier One SEL curriculum pilot at the elementary level; CSTAG self-harm trainings for school psychologists and social workers; a Middle School Advisory Study Team; a completed student code of conduct review; an emphasis on adult learning through NEP Day of Learning/ILT; and a 2022-23 Equity Analysis Survey with listening tours. Survey key findings and recommendations include diversifying and expanding the Red Pillar team around Alignment, Access, and Agency; expanding the SEL curriculum pilot; transforming adult SEL; running professional and community learning series with an equity focus; investigating wraparound services such as afterschool programs specific to SEL and equity; partnering with the Director of Security to review safety protocols; establishing consistent MTSS structures; and conducting book studies and workshop series on Culturally Responsive Teaching and Street Data.
